title: Take, Lord, receive
hookLine: Ignatius' prayer offering liberty, memory, understanding and will
carry: your love and grace are enough

lines: THE EXERCISES END WITH AN INVENTORY.
cards: The Spiritual Exercises end with an inventory.
After praying through the life of Jesus, start to finish, Ignatius of Loyola asks the one praying to count up gifts: being made at all, being redeemed, and everything particular to their own life.
Then he asks a question that sounds simple and isn't: given all that, what would you give back? His answer is a short prayer, known by its first word in Latin. Suscipe.
Receive. It's today's word, and it closes this stretch with Ignatius.

teach.h: LOVE SHOWS IN DEEDS, AND SHARES.
teach.b: Ignatius opens this last contemplation with two short notes about love. First, love shows itself more in deeds than in words.
Second, love is a sharing: the one who loves gives what they have to the beloved, and the beloved gives back. Then comes the prayer. In plain English, it runs like this.

Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, and my whole will, all that I have and possess. You gave it to me; to you, Lord, I return it. All of it is yours; do with it what you will.
Give me your love and your grace; that is enough for me. Look at what's offered. Not money, not achievements.
Freedom, memory, understanding, will: the inside of a person. And look at the reason.

teach.h: WHAT HAST THOU THAT THOU DIDST NOT RECEIVE?
teach.b: Paul asks the church at Corinth: "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" Nothing is handed over that wasn't a gift first. The request at the end is small on purpose: love and grace.
Paul hears something like it from Christ: "My grace is sufficient for thee."
That's where this week has been heading: a gospel scene stepped into, the king's call, two banners, the watch at the cross and the empty tomb, reading the drift inside, and not deciding in the dark.

teach.h: A WEEK THAT ENDS WITH A GIFT RETURNED.
teach.b: It all ends not with a technique, but with a gift handed back. This is a hard prayer to mean all the way through. Some teachers of the Exercises call it a prayer to grow into, not a test to pass.

how: The Suscipe comes at the end of the Spiritual Exercises, in the Contemplation to Attain Love; Jesuits and others shaped by Ignatian spirituality pray it on retreat and in daily prayer, and it has been set to music as a hymn.

games.q: at the end of the Exercises, Ignatius asks what you'd give back for everything you've received. what does the Suscipe offer?
games.why: the whole inside of a person, handed back, with only love and grace asked in return.

practice: Go slowly through the four, pausing on each: liberty, the freedom you have today; memory, what you carry; understanding, how you make sense of things; will, what you choose.
If you pray, say Ignatius' prayer phrase by phrase, offering each one back; if you don't, simply hold each gift for a moment and notice where it came from.
